title: Oracles against the Nations
lead: Most of the prophets have collections of words against foreign peoples (Isaiah 13–23; Jeremiah 46–51; Ezekiel 25–32; Amos 1–2; Obadiah; Nahum; Zephaniah 2). They were spoken mostly to Israel and Judah, to warn them off alliances and to promise that the LORD rules the nations too.

sections.b: Most of the prophetic books contain words addressed to or about foreign nations, often gathered into collections. The largest are Isaiah 13–23 (Babylon, Assyria, Philistia, Moab, Damascus, Cush, Egypt, Edom, Arabia, Jerusalem and Tyre), Jeremiah 46–51 (Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar, Elam and Babylon; in the Greek they stand after Jeremiah 25:13), and Ezekiel 25–32 (Ammon, Moab, Edom, Philistia, Tyre, Sidon and Egypt). Amos opens with a series against Israel's neighbors that ends with Judah and Israel (Amos 1:3–2:16). Obadiah is entirely about Edom, Nahum about Nineveh, and Zephaniah 2 and Zechariah 9 have shorter series. In the Hebrew order the collections often stand in the middle of a book, between oracles of judgment on Israel and oracles of hope.
sections.refs: Isaiah 13:1–23:18; Jeremiah 46:1–51:64; Ezekiel 25:1–32:32; Amos 1:3–2:16; Obadiah 1:1–21; Nahum 1:1–3:19; Zephaniah 2:4–15; Zechariah 9:1–8

sections.b: Although many oracles address a foreign nation directly ('Howl, ships of Tarshish!'), they were spoken in Israel and Judah and preserved there. Their hearers were God's people. They served several purposes. They warned Judah's kings not to trust foreign alliances (Isaiah 20; Isaiah 30:1–7). They assured a threatened people that the empires around them were under God's sentence. They declared that the LORD is not a local god but rules every nation and judges each for pride, cruelty and violence against others (Amos 1:3–2:3). And Amos used them as a trap: his hearers would agree with the judgment on their neighbors, until he turned to Judah and Israel. A few oracles may also have been sent abroad (Jeremiah 27:2–3; Jeremiah 51:59–64).
sections.refs: Isaiah 14:24–27; Isaiah 20:1–6; Isaiah 30:1–7; Jeremiah 27:2–11; Jeremiah 51:59–64; Amos 1:3–2:16

sections.b: Scholars trace the oracles against the nations to the ancient practice of cursing enemies before battle. Balaam is hired to curse Israel and instead blesses it and pronounces oracles on Moab, Edom, Amalek and the Kenites (Numbers 22–24). Egyptian 'execration texts' wrote the names of foreign rulers on pottery that was then smashed, and prophets at Mari on the Euphrates delivered oracles to the king about enemy rulers. John Hayes connected the biblical oracles with war and with worship, and Duane Christensen traced their growth from war oracles into prophetic preaching. The headings in Isaiah use massa', 'oracle'; other features are the summons to wail, the lament, the taunt song and the list of a nation's sins.

sections.h: What they teach: judgment and hope
sections.b: The oracles judge nations mainly for pride ('We have heard of Moab's pride', Isaiah 16:6), cruelty in war (Amos 1:3, 13) and violence against God's people (Obadiah 1:10–14). But several end with hope. Isaiah promises that Egypt and Assyria will worship with Israel (Isaiah 19:23–25) and that Tyre's profits will be holy to the LORD (Isaiah 23:18); Cush will bring gifts to Zion (Isaiah 18:7). Jeremiah promises that the LORD will restore the fortunes of Moab, Ammon and Elam (Jeremiah 48:47; Jeremiah 49:6; Jeremiah 49:39). The same God who humbles the nations intends their blessing, as he promised Abraham (Genesis 12:3).
sections.refs: Isaiah 16:6; Isaiah 18:7; Isaiah 19:23–25; Isaiah 23:18; Jeremiah 48:47; Jeremiah 49:6; Jeremiah 49:39; Amos 1:3; Genesis 12:3

sections.b: Readers disagree on how the oracles were fulfilled. Many were fulfilled in ancient history: Damascus fell to Assyria in 732 BC, Nineveh in 612 BC, Babylon to Cyrus in 539 BC, Tyre's island to Alexander in 332 BC. Some details of total ruin came only over centuries, or not literally (Babylon was taken without a battle). Critical scholars note that prophets reused and updated earlier oracles (Isaiah 16:13–14) and that some were written or expanded after the events. Some futurist readers expect further fulfillment for nations such as Babylon, Damascus or Edom at the end of the age. Others read the nations as types of every power that sets itself against God.
sections.refs: Isaiah 13:19–22; Isaiah 16:13–14; Isaiah 17:1; Nahum 3:1–7; Ezekiel 26:3–14; Ezekiel 29:18

sections.b: The New Testament reuses the oracles against the nations above all in Revelation. Its lament over 'Babylon the Great' (Revelation 18) weaves together Isaiah's and Jeremiah's oracles on Babylon and Ezekiel's on Tyre: 'Fallen! Fallen is Babylon the Great' (Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:2; Isaiah 21:9), the merchants and sailors standing far off (Revelation 18:11–19; Ezekiel 27). Jesus names Tyre, Sidon and Sodom as places that would have repented had they seen his works, and warns the towns of Galilee that judgment will be harder for them (Matthew 11:21–24). Christ is given 'the key of David' from Isaiah's oracle on Jerusalem (Revelation 3:7; Isaiah 22:22).
sections.refs: Revelation 14:8; Revelation 18:1–24; Isaiah 21:9; Isaiah 22:22; Revelation 3:7; Ezekiel 27:1–36; Matthew 11:21–24
